title: Sheet Metal Manufacturing
summary: Cutting, bending math (bend allowance, bend deduction), bend design rules, springback, tolerances, and nesting for sheet metal parts.

sections.heading: The Sheet Metal Process Chain
sections.content: Sheet metal fabrication turns flat stock into stiff, light, enclosure-capable parts through three core operations: **cutting** (separating), **forming** (bending, flanging), and **joining** (welding, fastening — see [[welding-and-joining|welding]]). The economics are excellent at medium volumes: fast cycles, low tooling for laser + press brake, and parts that are cheap to paint and assemble. The discipline is geometric: flat-blank math, bend-radius limits, and hole placement all get decided before the press brake ever runs.

sections.heading: Cutting: Punching, Laser & Waterjet
sections.content:
The cut defines the blank and every hole before forming:

- **Shearing / punching** — mechanical cut with a die; cheapest at volume, leaves a **burr** on one side and a shear zone; minimum hole diameter ~1.2× stock thickness in punching.
- **Laser cutting** — CO2/fiber: kerf 0.1–0.3 mm, edge quality classifiable (ISO 9013), excellent for prototypes and complex contours; heat-affected edge on thicker material.
- **Waterjet** — no heat-affected zone, cuts any material stack including thick plate; slower, more expensive per metre, square edges.
- **Edge quality**: burr height and direction matter for operator safety and for bends — the burr side takes the **tension** in bending better; place burrs accordingly.

Feature rules: minimum hole size, minimum slot width (~1×t), and **hole-to-edge distance ≥ 2×t** to prevent the hole distorting into the edge.

sections.heading: Bend Allowance & Flat-Blank Length
sections.content:
Bending stretches the outside and compresses the inside of the sheet around a **neutral axis** that shifts toward the inner face. The **bend allowance** is the arc length of the neutral axis over the bend:

$$BA = \theta \, \frac{\pi}{180} (R + K t)$$

with $K$ the K-factor (neutral-axis position as a fraction of thickness; 0.44 for air-bent mild steel, ~0.3 for tight-radius coining). Example — 90° bend, $R = 2$ mm, $t = 1.5$ mm, $K = 0.44$:

$$BA = 90 \times 0.01745 \times (2 + 0.44 \times 1.5) = 1.5708 \times 2.66 = 4.18 \text{ mm}$$

The **bend deduction** (how much to subtract from the sum of outside dimensions for the flat blank):

$$BD = 2(R + t) - BA$$

For the same bend: $BD = 2 \times 3.5 - 4.18 = 2.82$ mm. Every CAD sheet-metal module (see [[cad-computer-aided-design|CAD]]) computes this — but the K-factor must match the shop's tooling, or your "perfect" flat pattern is wrong by millimetres.

sections.heading: Bend Design Rules
sections.content:
Features adjacent to bends get distorted unless spaced properly:

- **Minimum bend radius** (air bend, mild steel ≈ 0.5–1.0×t; higher-strength and some stainless need 1.5–2×t; aluminium often 2×t). Below it, the outer fiber cracks.
- **Minimum flange length** ≈ 4×t + R — enough material for the die opening to grip.
- **Hole-to-bend distance** $d \geq 2.5t + R$ — holes inside the bend zone stretch into ovals; the rule keeps them clear of the deformation zone.
- **Notch/slot to bend** similar relief needed; add **relief cuts** at bend ends of flanges to prevent tearing.
- **Form height** ≥ 2×t for bends to be stable; tabs and lances need their own min dimensions.

Dimensioning bends: give the bend **inside radius** and the **outside flange dimensions** (what the operator measures) — never the neutral-axis lengths; and note **grain direction** for tight radii (bend across the rolling grain when possible).

sections.heading: Springback & Overbend
sections.content:
After the punch releases, the elastic portion of the deformation springs the sheet back toward flat. Springback grows with:

- **Higher strength** (high-strength steel, stainless, spring temper) — more elastic recovery.
- **Smaller thickness-to-radius ratios** (sharp bends in thin sheet spring back a lot).

Compensation tactics:

- **Overbend** — the punch angle, air-bend die geometry, or a heel on the tool makes the part spring back to the target angle.
- **Bottoming/coining** — pressing the sheet to the die bottom (or past yield locally) dramatically reduces springback scatter at the cost of tooling life.
- **Bend relief / stress reversal** — in critical cases, a secondary bending operation.

Springback is **scatter**, not just offset: the same nominal bend varies across sheets. For precision formed parts, measure the first pieces, adjust the program, and hold the process within the band — pressure-brake programs live and die by this feedback loop.

sections.heading: Tolerances & Nesting
sections.content:
Realistic sheet-metal tolerances (laser-cut parts):

- Cut profile (laser) ±0.1–0.2 mm; hole diameters ±0.1 mm.
- **Bend-to-hole** positions ±0.3 mm — the bend itself is the biggest uncertainty source; bend angles ±0.5° typical air-bend.
- **Formed part overall** ±0.5–1.0 mm across flange sets; the flat blank holds tighter than the formed result.

Do not carry machining-style tolerances (±0.02 mm) onto sheet metal — the process cannot hold them flat, and you will pay for it (see [[engineering-specifications|specification]] reality).

**Nesting** is the cost lever: place parts on the sheet to maximize **material utilization** (% of sheet turned into parts). Goals: common-line cutting (one cut shared by two parts), skeleton minimized, grain direction respected where required. Software nesting plus better layouts routinely lift utilization from 55% to 75%+ — at plate prices that is the difference between a profitable and a losing job.

keyTakeaways: Flat-blank length needs bend allowance math: BA = θ·(π/180)·(R + Kt), BD = 2(R+t) − BA.
Keep holes ≥ 2.5t + R from bends and flange lengths ≥ 4t + R, or features distort.
Springback is scatter: overbend or bottom to hold angles, and iterate from first-piece measurement.
Realistic tolerances: cut ±0.1–0.2 mm, bend-to-hole ±0.3 mm — not machining tolerances.
